title: Pow(x, n)
statement: Compute x raised to the integer power n, where x is a real number and n is an integer that can be negative, zero, or as big as about two billion. Write it without the built-in power function, and fast enough that multiplying n times is not an option.

example.caption: 2 to the 10 needs only four squarings. The bits of 10 are 1010, so keep the squares 4 and 256 and multiply them: 4 × 256 = 1024.

output.label: squares of x: x², x⁴, x⁸ (used are green)

idea.sentence: Write n in binary: x^n is the product of x^1, x^2, x^4, x^8 and so on for each 1 bit, and each of those is the previous one squared.

jargon.plain: Get x^(2k) from x^k with one multiplication (x^k times x^k), so the power doubles every step and n needs only about log2(n) steps.
One binary digit. The lowest bit of k tells you if k is odd. Dropping it is k divided by 2, rounded down.

watch.inputHint: Two arguments: x (a number) and n (an integer, may be negative). Keep x small and n modest, so the answer stays within normal float range.

compare.bruteLabel: Multiply x by itself n times
compare.optimalLabel: Square the base, one step per bit of n

rows.name: Multiply n times
rows.note: For n around two billion that is billions of steps, far too slow.

rows.name: Square the base
rows.note: n has about log2(n) bits, so at most 31 squarings and 31 multiplications for any 32-bit n.

fast.takeaway: Doubling the power each step turns two billion steps into about 31. The same trick powers modular arithmetic in cryptography.

variants.label: Square on the bits of n

stages.title: Set up
stages.note: result = 1. If n is negative, replace x by 1/x and n by its absolute value, so k is never negative.

stages.title: Bit is 1: multiply
stages.note: If the lowest bit of k is 1, the current base is one of the factors. Multiply it into the result.

stages.title: Square and shift
stages.note: Square the base, drop the lowest bit of k, repeat until k is 0.

edges.title: Power zero
edges.why: The loop never runs and result stays 1. This holds for every x, even 0 by the usual convention.

edges.title: Negative power
edges.why: Flip to 1/2 = 0.5 and square it. A negative n is just the reciprocal of the positive power.

edges.title: Smallest 32-bit n
edges.why: The true answer is far below the smallest float, so it underflows to 0. The code must not crash while negating n.

edges.title: Base 1 or -1 with a huge n
edges.why: The loop takes only 31 turns. The first bit multiplies in -1, then the base squares to 1, so every later bit multiplies in 1.

gotchas.text: n = -2147483648 has no positive twin in 32 bits. Writing n = -n there overflows back to the same negative number and the loop never runs. Languages with 32-bit ints must widen to 64 bits first.
JS numbers are doubles, so Math.abs(-2147483648) is fine. But k >> 1 and k | 0 first convert to a 32-bit int, which turns 2147483648 into a negative number. Use Math.floor(k / 2), not shifts.
Math.pow and ** exist and are correct, but the exercise asks you to write the loop. Also remember 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3: powers of floats carry tiny errors, so compare answers with a tolerance.
A negative x with an underflowing power can print as -0. -0 === 0 is true, but Object.is(-0, 0) is false and a test that expects 0 may complain.
int is 64 bits on 64-bit machines, so n = -n is safe for any 32-bit n there. With int32 it would overflow just like in C. Go has no ** operator, and math.Pow exists but hides the idea.

recap.key: Walk the bits of n from the lowest. Multiply the base into the result on every 1 bit, and square the base every turn.
moves: While k > 0: if k is odd, result *= base
base *= base; k = k / 2 (drop the lowest bit)
